title: Reserved capacity safety, eviction behavior and queueing for Argon Systems
summary: Deep dive on reserved GPU safety nets, eviction and prewarm behavior, queueing/backpressure modeling, KV cache warmup, batching and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a targeted latency benchmark, share reserved capacity playbook and security checklist; customer to provide peak QPS profile and model artifact list.
topics: KV cache warmup and prefix caching
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: ok everyone's on, hey Lina, Marcus, Anika. thanks for carving time. we're Maya (AE) and Daniel (SE) from Redwood. this call is to walk through reserved capacity safety, eviction behavior and how burst policies interact with kv cache warming and batching.
[00:22] Lina: thanks Maya. we have a hard latency SLO on our customer-facing assistants, 95th percentile under 350ms for short prompts. we also see big spikes midday, like 4x baseline for 10-15 minutes. we're evaluating reserved GPUs but worried about paying for headroom and what happens if the reserved pool is saturated.
[00:39] Daniel: yeah totally, good constraints. quick question on traffic shape — is the spike traffic many short requests or a few heavy long-context ones?
[00:47] Anika: mostly short — ~20–80 token prompts, but we also run larger summarization jobs at night. for the spikes it's a lot of small chat messages, high concurrency.
[00:58] Marcus: and security wise we need VPC peering and bring-your-own-kms. can you remind us how Redwood's private handles kms/hsm integrations with reserved capacity?
[01:10] Maya: short answer: supported. for Private/VPC customers we integrate with your KMS or HSM and tokens never leave the VPC egress. we'll share the security checklist after. Daniel will get into details.
[01:22] Daniel: on eviction and safety: reserved pools are pre-provisioned GPUs that you commit to. we provide eviction policies in two layers — graceful drain at the request router and an autoscale overlay that can borrow from shared burst if allowed. if your pool is full we can queue at the router with backpressure, or if you have burst enabled we'll route to a compatible cheaper variant (smaller quant, different instance) depending on policy.
[01:46] Lina: that routing fallback — does it change tokenization or response shape? worried about hallucination/regression.
[01:53] Daniel: good call. by default we try to route to model variants that are functionally equivalent (same family, quantized but validated). there's also a policy flag to disallow fallback for critical paths. we recommend canarying fallback across 1–5% of traffic and running evals against your prompt suite.
[02:09] Marcus: how long does kv cache warming take after a model switch or fallback? our assistants rely heavily on prefix cache to keep latency down.
[02:18] Daniel: warmup depends on your prefix reuse rate. with continuous prefix caching we see effective warmup in tens of seconds for common conversational flows; cold start for a new shard can be multiple round trips and add 100–300ms depending on token length. we have automatic prewarming hooks if you pass active session ids at deploy time.
[02:40] Anika: are those hooks available in Private/VPC?
[02:44] Daniel: yes, same API surface. for on-prem we provide an agent that can run warmup scripts within your network so no traffic leaves your environment.
[02:53] [small crosstalk — someone drops connection briefly]
[03:05] Maya: let's talk queueing. for short prompt spiky workloads the M/M/c approximation is useful to get a feel for tail latency under concurrency. Daniel, can you talk through an example?
[03:15] Daniel: sure. if you have N GPUs each with concurrency c (slots for continuous batching), effective service rate mu is tokens per second per slot. arrival rate lambda is requests per second. for our customers hitting 4x spikes, the relevant metric is utilization rho = lambda / (c * N * mu). once rho approaches ~0.7–0.8 tail latency grows nonlinearly. we recommend reserved capacity sized for steady-state at ~0.5–0.7 and burst policy to absorb 2–3x short spikes.
[03:46] Lina: so you recommend we size fewer reserved GPUs and rely on burst?
[03:51] Daniel: it's tradeoff. sizing for steady-state saves money but you must accept potential fallback or higher queueing for rare spikes. reserved + burst with prewarmed ephemeral pools is common: keep a small prewarmed pool (1–2 nodes worth) and a larger cold-burst capacity that can spin up with ~30–90s depending on cloud and instance type.
[04:10] Marcus: that start time sounds long — our SLO window is tight. can prewarming reduce that to zero?
[04:15] Daniel: prewarming reduces warmup to near zero for model weights and kernels, but kv cache is per-session; you still need prefix warmup. we can provide a distributed warmup script that concurrently replays common prefixes to populate KV across shards before you route production traffic. for really tight SLOs some customers maintain a small always-on reserved buffer sized for worst-case short spikes.
[04:39] Anika: curious about batching — how does batching affect 95th percentile for short prompts? we worry batching increases latency.
[04:46] Daniel: dynamic batching is latency-aware. the runtime will cap hold time based on SLOs; for short prompts batching often improves throughput without hurting median, but can increase tail slightly if you allow high batch sizes. we expose batch window config: e.g., 5–15ms hold time tends to be sweet for sub-100-token chats.
[05:05] Lina: quantization — can we use 4-bit for most inference? how does it affect hallucination vs throughput?
[05:12] Daniel: 4-bit quant (Q4 variants) gives 2–3x throughput, but model-specific. we validate on a customer's eval set. in our experience for many chat workloads Q4_K_M style quant retains quality for small prompts, but for long-context summarizations we prefer Q8 or fp16. we can provide quantization recommendation per model + accuracy delta report.
[05:33] Marcus: and in Private, do you handle kernel/compilation locally? i'm thinking about A100 vs H100 differences.
[05:39] Daniel: runtime picks kernels based on detected hardware; in Private we ship a compilation layer that caches kernels. H100 gives better throughput for certain attention kernels, but you get diminishing returns for short token workloads. we'll run an H100 vs A100 micro-benchmark against your model set.
[05:58] Anika: what's the behavior when reserved pool is at capacity and a low-priority internal job is scheduled? is it preempted?
[06:05] Daniel: reserved has tenancy rules. jobs marked as "low-priority" can be preempted in favor of higher-priority customer traffic. we support priority classes and graceful draining. you can also configure eviction windows — e.g., allow eviction only outside business hours.
[06:18] Lina: one more on auditing — we need audit logs for all routing decisions and KMS key usage.
[06:23] Maya: we have detailed trace logs, per-request routing reason codes and KMS call records. we'll attach the sample schema.
[06:30] [15m mark — participant asks for clarifications on numbers]
[06:32] Marcus: give me a concrete example: we have 10k RPS baseline 95% are short chat at 20 tokens, spike to 40k for 10 minutes. what's a practical reserved + burst config?
[06:45] Daniel: quickback-of-envelope: assume token-generation rate ~1000 tokens/sec per GPU slot for that model at Q4; with average 20 tokens, that's ~50 req/sec per slot. with GPU concurrency 8 slots you get ~400 req/sec per GPU. so to support 10k steady you'd need ~25 GPUs steady. for 40k spikes you'd need 100 GPUs, so you could reserve 25 and rely on burst to supply additional 75. prewarm a small buffer (~10 GPUs) to keep tail low while cold burst spins up.
[07:20] Lina: interesting. can Redwood simulate that with our real traces?
[07:24] Daniel: yes we can run a capacity simulation if you provide a 24h trace (anonymized). we'll model warmup, batch distributions, and predict 95/99 latencies for various policies.
[07:34] Anika: what's the expected cost delta if we reserve 25 vs reserve 40 GPUs?
[07:39] Maya: we'll send a cost model spreadsheet. rough rule: reserved reduces unit compute cost by ~15–35% depending on commitment term; but you pay for headroom. the spreadsheet will show TCO including burst-on-demand costs.
[07:52] [small pause — someone checks doc link]
[07:58] Marcus: about fallback variants — do you keep quantized variants in the same pool or separate pools? curious about routing latency when switching.
[08:06] Daniel: typically separate pools. switching to a quantized variant can be near-instant if the variant is already warm; if not, warming is needed. we also support multi-variant bundles where binaries live on the same node which speeds switching.
[08:21] Lina: how do you validate fallback quality? we need to ensure hallucination doesn't spike.
[08:26] Daniel: we recommend running a small suite of regression prompts continuously. Redwood Optimize can run these and alert on drift. during canary we measure embedding similarity, BLEU-like exact match and a human check for critical flows.
[08:41] Anika: timeline — we're aiming to decide on capacity approach in 3 weeks. can you deliver benchmarks and a recommended sizing plan within that time?
[08:49] Maya: yes — deliverables: 1) reserved capacity playbook for Argon, 2) security checklist + KMS integration notes, 3) simulated capacity report from your trace, 4) cost spreadsheet, 5) targeted latency benchmark. can we align a follow up next week for benchmark kickoff?
[09:04] Lina: yes let's do next Tuesday.
[09:08] Marcus: action items — we'll send a 24h anonymized trace and list of model artifacts. also need a contact for infra to open a VPC peering request.
[09:18] Maya: noted.
[09:20] [wrap up and recap]
[09:22] Maya: recap — we'll run simulation and bench, share playbook and security docs, propose reserved+prewarm config and cost. next: schedule kickoff — Daniel will run the trace sim. Lina will send the trace and infra contact.
[09:36] Daniel: quick technical note — for prefix-heavy sessions consider sticky routing to keep KV locality; it slightly reduces global load balancing flexibility but improves tail latency.
[09:48] Lina: thanks team. that sticky routing — is that supported in Private?
[09:52] Daniel: yep, supported via session affinity tokens.
[09:56] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with links and calendar invite. end of call.
